w: Joze Plecnik spent most of the 1930s turning an ordinary riverside market into an arcaded colonnade running the length of the Ljubljanica, from the Triple Bridge to the Dragon Bridge. Stallholders still sell produce under his arches every morning -- a national monument that never stopped being a market.
s: A working market designed by Plecnik
_facts: Osrednja ljubljanska tržnica, riverside market building designed by Jože Plečnik 1931-1939
Stretches between the Triple Bridge and the Dragon Bridge on the right bank of the Ljubljanica
The marketplace and Vodnik Square are cultural monuments of national significance

w: Rudolf Maister was a poet who became Slovenia's first-ever general almost by accident, mustering a scratch force in 1918 that secured Maribor for the new state before anyone else could claim it. This bronze, sculpted by Jakov Brdar in 1999, puts him on horseback outside the railway station.
_facts: Bronze equestrian statue of Rudolf Maister at Liberation Front Square, in front of Ljubljana railway station
Tribute to Maister, the first Slovene major general, who secured the city of Maribor for Slovenia

w: Probably raised in the 11th century and rebuilt more than once since, this is the fortress the lords of Carniola ruled from before it settled into centuries of duller jobs as barracks, prison and grain store. It still watches over the city from its hill, dragon and all, on Ljubljana's own coat of arms.
s: The fortress on the city's coat of arms
_facts: Castle complex on Castle Hill above downtown Ljubljana, probably built 11th century, rebuilt 12th
Present outline dates to a 15th-century overhaul; most standing buildings are 16th-17th century
Since the early 14th century seat of the lords of Carniola; depicted on the city's coat of arms with a dragon

w: Named for the four dragon statues that flank its corners, this reinforced-concrete crossing over the Ljubljanica dates from the last years of Austro-Hungarian rule in the city. It counts among the finest examples of Vienna Secession engineering anywhere, and is protected today as a technical monument.
s: Named for the dragons guarding its corners
_facts: Zmajski most, road bridge crossing the Ljubljanica, built in the early 20th century under Austro-Hungarian rule
Regarded as one of the finest examples of reinforced-concrete bridges and of the Vienna Secession style
Protected today as a technical monument

w: Slovenia's largest cemetery spreads across the Bezigrad district, big enough to need its own dedicated public company just to run it. Everyone in Ljubljana simply calls it Zale -- the plain, unglamorous name for the place where the whole capital eventually ends up.
_facts: The largest and central cemetery in Ljubljana and Slovenia
Operated by the Žale Public Company

w: Rebuilt after the 1895 earthquake, this courthouse became a stage for Yugoslavia's postwar reckonings -- the Rozman, Nagode and Dachau trials of the late 1940s put opponents of the new Titoist regime in the dock here. The verdicts were often decided before the trials began; the building just supplied the theatre.
s: Site of Yugoslavia's postwar show trials
_facts: Sodna palača, 19th-century courthouse built after the 1895 earthquake, renovated in the early 1950s
In the late 1940s hosted show trials against opponents of the Yugoslav Titoist regime: the Rožman trial (1945), Nagode trial (1946) and Dachau trials (1947)
